title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models

covered_actors: National data protection supervisory authorities (SAs) in the EEA
Data controllers developing or deploying AI models trained with personal data

evidence.quote: Data protection impact assessments (“DPIAs”) (Articles 35 GDPR): DPIAs are an important element of accountability, where the processing in the context of AI models is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
By default, SAs should consider that AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification to reach a conclusion on their possible anonymous nature.
evidence.source_section: 3.2.1 General consideration regarding anonymisation in the context at hand

evidence.quote: At to the date of this Opinion, this could include, among others, structured testing against: (i) attribute and membership inference; (ii) exfiltration; (iii) regurgitation of training data; (iv) model inversion; or (v) reconstruction attacks.
evidence.source_section: 3.2.2.3 AI model testing and resistance to attacks

evidence.quote: Considering the complexity of the technologies involved, information on the processing of personal data within AI models should therefore be provided in an accessible, understandable and user-friendly way

Release of public and easily accessible communications which go beyond the information required under Article 13 or 14 GDPR, for instance by providing additional details about the collection criteria and all datasets used, taking into account special protection for children and vulnerable persons.

Articles 5, 24, 25, and 30 GDPR, and, in cases of likely high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, Article 35 GDPR, require controllers to adequately document their processing operations. This also applies to any processing that would include the training of an AI model, even if the objective of the processing is anonymisation.

the documentation demonstrating the AI model’s theoretical resistance to re-identification techniques, as well as the controls designed to limit or assess the success and impact of main attacks (regurgitation, membership inference attacks, exfiltration, etc.).

SAs should evaluate whether controllers have conducted any document-based audits (internal or external) that include an evaluation of the chosen measures and of their impact to limit the likelihood of identification.

Technical measures may for instance be put in place to prevent the storage, regurgitation or generation of personal data, especially in the context of generative AI models (such as output filters), and/or to mitigate the risk of unlawful reuse by general purpose AI models (e.g. digital watermarking of AI-generated outputs).
In accordance with the data minimisation principle, the development and deployment of AI models requires that personal data should be adequate, relevant and necessary in relation to the purpose.

Excluding collection from websites (or sections of websites) which clearly object to web scraping and the reuse of their content for the purpose of building AI training databases (for example, by respecting robots.txt or ai.txt files or any other recognised mechanism to express exclusion from automated crawling or scraping).
It is, therefore, within the competence of SAs to investigate specific AI models and, in doing so, to conduct case-by-case assessments.

When there is the finding of an infringement, SAs may impose corrective measures, such as ordering controllers, taking into account the circumstances of each case, to take actions in order to remediate the unlawfulness of the initial processing.
evidence.source_section: 3.4 On the possible impact of an unlawful processing in the development of an AI model on the lawfulness of the subsequent processing or operation of the AI model

evidence.quote: These may include, for instance, issuing a fine, imposing a temporary limitation on the processing, erasing part of the dataset that was processed unlawfully or, where this is not possible, depending on the facts at hand, having regard to the proportionality of the measure, ordering the erasure of the whole dataset used to develop the AI model and/or the AI model itself.
evidence.source_section: 3.4 On the possible impact of an unlawful processing in the development of an AI model on the lawfulness of the subsequent processing or operation of the AI model

evidence.quote: imposing a temporary limitation on the processing, erasing part of the dataset that was processed unlawfully or, where this is not possible, depending on the facts at hand, having regard to the proportionality of the measure, ordering the erasure of the whole dataset used to develop the AI model and/or the AI model itself.

enforcement_authorities: National data protection supervisory authorities (SAs) in the EEA
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Under Article 58 GDPR, national supervisory authorities enjoy discretionary powers to impose appropriate, necessary, and proportionate corrective measures upon finding an infringement, including issuing administrative fines, imposing temporary limitations on processing, ordering ex officio erasure of unlawfully processed personal data or part of the training dataset, or—where necessary and proportionate—ordering the erasure of the entire training dataset and/or the AI model itself, without prejudice to enforcement under the EU AI Act or civil liability frameworks.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Adopted pursuant to Article 64(2) GDPR following a 4 September 2024 request from the Irish supervisory authority, this Opinion is addressed to all EEA supervisory authorities to promote consistent GDPR application across the EEA. It provides a non-exhaustive, case-by-case analytical framework on AI model anonymity, legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR) in development and deployment, and the downstream consequences of unlawful training data processing, without prejudice to controllers' and processors' existing GDPR obligations. It explicitly excludes detailed analysis of special categories of data (Article 9), automated decision-making (Article 22), purpose compatibility (Article 6(4)), DPIAs (Article 35), and data protection by design (Article 25), and notes forthcoming EDPB guidelines on anonymisation, pseudonymisation, and data scraping for generative AI.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The Opinion is overwhelmingly framed around fundamental_rights, as the EDPB interprets GDPR provisions to protect data subjects' EU Charter rights—specifically privacy (Article 7), personal data protection (Article 8), freedom of expression (Article 11), non-discrimination (Article 21), and self-determination—throughout AI model development and deployment. While innovation_enablement appears as a secondary rationale in the preamble and admissibility section (characterizing GDPR as a framework that supports AI opportunities and encourages responsible innovation through consistent supervisory application) and consumer_public_safety appears in the balancing test (citing risks of fraud, phishing, deepfakes, physical/mental harm, and manipulation of vulnerable individuals), both remain subordinate to the document's core legal mandate of safeguarding individual fundamental rights and freedoms.

evidence_spans.quote: By protecting the fundamental right to data protection, GDPR supports these opportunities and promotes other EU fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of thought, expression and information, the right to education or the freedom to conduct a business.

In relation to the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subjects, the development and deployment of AI models may raise serious risks to rights protected by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (the “EU Charter”), including, but not limited to, the right to private and family life (Article 7 EU Charter) and the right to protection of personal data (Article 8 EU Charter).
Additionally, AI technologies create many opportunities and benefits across a wide range of sectors and social activities. Besides, GDPR is a legal framework that encourages responsible innovation.

deployment of AI models may also present risks to the security and safety of the individual (e.g. where the AI model is used with malicious intent), as well as risks to their physical and mental integrity

this may include controls limiting as much as possible their use for harmful practices, for instance: the creation of deepfakes; chatbots that are used for disinformation, phishing and other types of fraud; and manipulative AI/AI agents
